Competition day: sleep, coffee, water and food

An international Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ competition is 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25, often over several days (Chapter 16 · 200 targets in rounds of 25). A round of Compak® Sporting is 25 targets, five at each station (Chapter 17 · A round: 25 targets, 5 per station). A day at the ground can last from morning to evening, with walking, waiting, sun and wind.

When your head is tired, you aim less well and react more slowly. Between stands, switch off: talk, drink, sit in the shade, and add up your score later.

Some research

The night before: go to bed at your usual time and allow a sleep window of 7–9 hours. Pack your kit and write down tomorrow's plan, so you do not lie awake going over it.

Some research

Poor sleep before an important event is common: in one survey, about 64% of athletes slept worse. If you cannot sleep, rest calmly. The nights before matter too, so sleep well during the week.

Some research

Coffee: stick to your usual amount and do not try more on the day. In one study with competition shooters (not clay shooters), a large dose (300 mg, about as much caffeine as three or four cups of brewed coffee) made their scores worse. So extra caffeine is unlikely to help.

Little research

Stop caffeine early in the day: half of it is still in your body about 5 hours later, and it can spoil your sleep. Energy drinks can add tremor and nerves.

Some research

Water: drink a little and often through the day, not only when you are very thirsty. In studies, losing more than about 2% of your body weight in fluid (about 1.5 litres for someone of 75 kg) made people less attentive and less precise. On hot days you may need more.

Some research

Food: a familiar breakfast 2–3 hours before shooting, then small snacks at 60–90 minute intervals on a long day. A heavy meal just before a round can make you sleepy, and hunger makes it hard to focus. Do not try new foods on the day.

Coaches' experience

Safety: Wash your hands before you eat at the ground: they can carry lead from cartridges and empties. More in Lead and hygiene.

Safety: No alcohol before or during shooting, including the lunch break. Alcohol slows reactions and affects coordination and sleep, and alcohol and guns do not mix. Ground rules and national law may forbid it too.

Some research

Note that alcohol has not been on the WADA Prohibited List since 1 January 2018 (WADA is the World Anti-Doping Agency, which sets the list of substances banned in sport). That is not permission: keep evening drinks away from nights before shooting days.

A long drive or flight tires you more than you expect: stiff muscles, dry air, little movement. If you can, arrive the day before, walk a little and drink water. Flying across time zones adds jet lag: see Jet lag and the first days at a new ground.

Coaches' experience

Tip: Pack a day kit: water, snacks, a cap, a warm layer and a rain jacket. Then at the ground you think about targets, not about where to find water.

Coaches' experience

Tip: If you organise a tour or a club day, plan shade, water and snacks near the layouts, and avoid late dinners or alcohol events before shooting days.

Coaches' experience

Key points

  • The night before: usual bedtime, kit packed, plan written down.
  • Coffee: your usual amount, and not late in the day.
  • Carry water and drink small sips through the day.
  • Familiar breakfast, small snacks; wash your hands before eating.
  • No alcohol before or during shooting.

Did you know?

Caffeine is not banned in sport: WADA only keeps an eye on how much athletes use. For a shooter the question is not the rules but steady hands and good sleep.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How can you drink water at the ground?

    1. In small sips through the day
    2. Only when you are very thirsty
    3. A lot at once, in the evening
    Answer

    In small sips through the day

    Small, regular sips help you avoid the fluid loss that affects attention.

  2. How much coffee on competition day?

    1. A large extra dose for focus
    2. Your usual amount, not late in the day
    3. None at all, because caffeine is prohibited
    Answer

    Your usual amount, not late in the day

    Keep your habit: a large dose can make the hands less steady, and caffeine is not prohibited.

  3. Why wash your hands before a snack at the ground?

    1. Because the referee requires it
    2. So that the gun does not slip in your hands
    3. They may carry lead from cartridges
    Answer

    They may carry lead from cartridges

    Lead often reaches the body through dirty hands and food.

This is not medical advice.
